nodes.title: What philosophy and logic are actually doing
outcomes: Distinguish philosophical inquiry from mere opinion-reporting and explain how claims, reasons, objections, and logical evaluation interact.

nodes.title: Questions, claims, reasons, and arguments
outcomes: Turn an open question into a candidate claim supported by explicit reasons.

nodes.title: Premises, conclusions, and argument indicators
outcomes: Identify premises and conclusions without mistaking indicator words for infallible rules.

nodes.title: Truth, validity, and soundness
outcomes: Separate whether premises are true from whether a conclusion follows and whether a deductive argument is sound.

nodes.title: Deduction, induction, and abduction
outcomes: Distinguish deductive support from ampliative inductive and abductive reasoning.

nodes.title: Counterexamples and testing universal claims
outcomes: Use a counterexample to refute a universal claim or an invalid inference pattern.

nodes.title: Ambiguity, vagueness, and conceptual distinctions
outcomes: Diagnose ambiguity and vagueness and introduce distinctions that improve a philosophical question.

nodes.title: Definitions and conceptual analysis
outcomes: Compare stipulative, lexical, and analytic uses of definitions without assuming every concept has a simple essence.

nodes.title: Principle of charity and steelmanning
outcomes: Reconstruct a position in a defensible form before criticizing it.

nodes.title: Informal fallacies as failed reasoning patterns
outcomes: Diagnose recurrent reasoning failures by explaining what goes wrong rather than matching labels mechanically.

nodes.title: Reading philosophy: thesis, argument, objection, reply
outcomes: Annotate a short philosophical passage into thesis, support, objection, and response.

nodes.title: Writing philosophy: claim, reason, objection, response
outcomes: Write a compact philosophical paragraph that states a claim, supports it, faces an objection, and responds.

nodes.title: What formalization gains and loses
outcomes: Explain why formalization can expose structure while also abstracting away context and meaning.

nodes.title: Propositions and truth-functional structure
outcomes: Recognize propositions as truth-evaluable contents and identify simple truth-functional structure.

nodes.title: Negation, conjunction, disjunction, and conditional
outcomes: Read the core propositional connectives in ordinary language and symbolic form.

nodes.title: Truth tables and semantic evaluation
outcomes: Evaluate simple truth-functional expressions with truth tables.

nodes.title: Predicates and quantifiers: first intuition
outcomes: Distinguish names, predicates, and quantifier-like expressions before formal predicate logic.

nodes.title: A map of philosophy: knowledge, reality, value, mind, language, science, and society
outcomes: Place a philosophical question into major fields while recognizing that real problems cross field boundaries.

nodes.title: Propositional-logic syntax and well-formed formulas
outcomes: Parse and construct well-formed propositional formulas.

nodes.title: Propositional semantics and valuations
outcomes: Evaluate formulas under valuations and distinguish syntax from semantics.

nodes.title: Testing propositional validity with truth tables
outcomes: Test propositional arguments for semantic validity.

nodes.title: Natural deduction: introduction and elimination rules
outcomes: Construct elementary natural-deduction proofs.

nodes.title: Proof strategy, subproofs, and contradiction
outcomes: Choose proof strategies and manage assumptions and subproofs.

nodes.title: The language of first-order logic
outcomes: Translate simple quantified claims into first-order form.

nodes.title: Quantifiers, scope, and bound variables
outcomes: Reason correctly about quantifier scope and variable binding.

nodes.title: Identity and definite description problems
outcomes: Use identity in formal arguments and recognize limits of naive translation.

nodes.title: First-order semantics: domains and interpretations
outcomes: Evaluate first-order sentences relative to domains and interpretations.

nodes.title: Argument reconstruction and hidden premises
outcomes: Reconstruct enthymematic real-world arguments while marking supplied assumptions.

nodes.title: Causal, statistical, and explanatory reasoning
outcomes: Distinguish correlation, causal claims, explanation, and evidential support.

nodes.title: Epistemology: knowledge, belief, truth, and justification
outcomes: Frame core questions about knowledge and justified belief.

nodes.title: Skepticism and responses to skeptical arguments
outcomes: Reconstruct a skeptical argument and compare major response strategies.

nodes.title: Perception, memory, testimony, and other epistemic sources
outcomes: Evaluate multiple proposed sources of knowledge and their vulnerabilities.

nodes.title: Metaphysics: what exists and what categories reality has
outcomes: Formulate ontological questions and distinguish existence questions from verbal disputes.

nodes.title: Identity and persistence through change
outcomes: Compare criteria of identity and persistence across time.

nodes.title: Causation, necessity, possibility, and free will
outcomes: Distinguish several metaphysical dependence and modality questions.

nodes.title: Normative ethics: consequences, duties, and virtues
outcomes: Compare consequentialist, deontological, and virtue-ethical reasoning.

nodes.title: Metaethics: what moral claims mean and whether they can be true
outcomes: Distinguish normative ethics from metaethical questions.

nodes.title: Political philosophy: justice, liberty, equality, and legitimacy
outcomes: Analyze conflicts among justice, liberty, equality, rights, and political legitimacy.

nodes.title: Philosophy of mind: mind, body, consciousness, and computation
outcomes: Compare major mind-body positions and frame the problem of consciousness.

nodes.title: Philosophy of language: meaning, reference, and communication
outcomes: Distinguish meaning, reference, truth conditions, and communicative use.

nodes.title: Philosophy of science: explanation, evidence, laws, and realism
outcomes: Frame philosophical questions about scientific explanation, evidence, and realism.

nodes.title: Ancient Greek philosophy: argument from the Presocratics through Aristotle
outcomes: Read ancient Greek positions as arguments rather than as lists of historical doctrines.

nodes.title: Classical Indian philosophy: knowledge sources, self, reality, and debate
outcomes: Recognize major Indian philosophical questions and methods without reducing them to Western categories.

nodes.title: Classical Chinese philosophy: ethics, order, language, and cultivation
outcomes: Compare argument and practical reasoning across major classical Chinese traditions.

nodes.title: Islamic philosophy: reason, revelation, metaphysics, and knowledge
outcomes: Locate major Islamic philosophical problems in their own intellectual contexts and later cross-tradition influence.

nodes.title: Early modern philosophy: rationalism, empiricism, mind, and world
outcomes: Compare early modern strategies for grounding knowledge and explaining mind-world relations.

nodes.title: Kant and the post-Kantian turn
outcomes: Explain why Kant reframes questions about knowledge, experience, and metaphysics.

nodes.title: Sets, relations, and functions for logic
outcomes: Use elementary set, relation, and function language needed by metalogic.

nodes.title: First-order natural deduction
outcomes: Construct and diagnose quantified natural-deduction proofs.

nodes.title: Soundness and completeness: what the theorems say
outcomes: Distinguish proof-theoretic derivability from semantic consequence and state the role of soundness and completeness.

nodes.title: Models and elementary model-theoretic reasoning
outcomes: Reason about satisfiability, models, countermodels, and elementary model-theoretic ideas.

nodes.title: Computability and effective procedure: philosophical foundations
outcomes: Explain the problem an effective-procedure notion solves and connect it to computability.

nodes.title: Gödel incompleteness: statement, scope, and common misreadings
outcomes: State incompleteness at an appropriate level and reject common overextensions.

nodes.title: Modal logic: necessity, possibility, and possible-world semantics
outcomes: Evaluate basic modal formulas and relate modality to philosophical use.

nodes.title: Probability and Bayesian reasoning for philosophers
outcomes: Use conditional probability and Bayes-style updating conceptually in evidential reasoning.

nodes.title: Argumentation, dialogue, burden of proof, and disagreement
outcomes: Analyze reasoning as an exchange with burdens, challenges, and responses.

nodes.title: Theories of epistemic justification
outcomes: Compare internalist, externalist, reliabilist, and virtue-epistemic strategies.

nodes.title: Gettier problems and the analysis of knowledge
outcomes: Explain why justified true belief faces Gettier-style counterexamples and compare repair strategies.

nodes.title: Social epistemology, testimony, expertise, and institutions
outcomes: Evaluate epistemic dependence on other people, experts, groups, and institutions.

nodes.title: Formal epistemology: credence, coherence, and updating
outcomes: Connect formal models of credence to philosophical questions about rational belief.

nodes.title: Universals, particulars, properties, and kinds
outcomes: Compare realist and nominalist approaches to properties and kinds.

nodes.title: Modality and possible worlds in metaphysics
outcomes: Use possible-world language while distinguishing semantics from metaphysical commitment.

nodes.title: Time, persistence, and temporal parts
outcomes: Compare major accounts of persistence and temporal ontology.

nodes.title: Grounding, dependence, essence, and explanation
outcomes: Distinguish causal explanation from proposed metaphysical dependence relations.

nodes.title: Philosophy of religion: arguments, evidence, evil, and faith
outcomes: Reconstruct central arguments in philosophy of religion without presupposing a religious conclusion.

nodes.title: Comparing consequentialism, deontology, virtue ethics, and contractualism
outcomes: Compare normative frameworks on shared cases and expose differences in justificatory structure.

nodes.title: Applied ethics: moving from principles to cases
outcomes: Analyze a concrete ethical problem while making factual and normative assumptions explicit.

nodes.title: Aesthetics and philosophy of art
outcomes: Frame questions about aesthetic value, interpretation, authorship, and art status.

nodes.title: Philosophy of law: rules, authority, interpretation, and responsibility
outcomes: Distinguish legal validity, moral evaluation, interpretation, and responsibility.

nodes.title: Functionalism, computation, and mental representation
outcomes: Evaluate computational and functional accounts of mind.

nodes.title: Perception, intentionality, and mental content
outcomes: Compare theories of perception and mental content.

nodes.title: Personal identity and the self
outcomes: Compare bodily, psychological, and other continuity criteria for personal identity.

nodes.title: Theories of meaning and reference
outcomes: Compare descriptivist, causal, use-based, and truth-conditional approaches.

nodes.title: Speech acts, implicature, and pragmatics
outcomes: Distinguish sentence meaning from speaker meaning and pragmatic inference.

nodes.title: Scientific realism and anti-realism
outcomes: Compare realism and anti-realism about theories, entities, and observable evidence.

nodes.title: Scientific explanation, causation, models, and mechanisms
outcomes: Compare major models of scientific explanation and the role of causation and mechanisms.

nodes.title: Philosophy of mathematics: truth, objects, proof, and applicability
outcomes: Frame foundational positions about mathematical objects, truth, proof, and application.

nodes.title: Analytic philosophy: language, logic, analysis, and their critics
outcomes: Trace major analytic projects while separating historical influence from endorsement.

nodes.title: Continental traditions: phenomenology, existentialism, hermeneutics, and critique
outcomes: Orient major continental approaches around their questions and methods rather than slogans.

nodes.title: African and Africana philosophy: personhood, knowledge, liberation, and method
outcomes: Engage African and Africana philosophical debates without treating the category as monolithic.

nodes.title: Feminist philosophy: knowledge, power, embodiment, and social categories
outcomes: Analyze how feminist philosophy reshapes epistemic, ethical, and metaphysical questions.

nodes.title: Modal proof systems and Kripke semantics
outcomes: Relate modal proof systems to Kripke frames and validity.

nodes.title: Intuitionistic logic and constructive reasoning
outcomes: Explain how intuitionistic consequence differs from classical consequence.

nodes.title: Many-valued and fuzzy logics
outcomes: Distinguish many-valued and fuzzy approaches from ordinary binary classical semantics.

nodes.title: Paraconsistent and relevance logics
outcomes: Explain motivations for logics that revise explosion or relevance conditions.

nodes.title: Temporal, deontic, and epistemic modal logics
outcomes: Model time, obligation, and knowledge with modal extensions while tracking interpretation assumptions.

nodes.title: Model theory beyond the basics
outcomes: Work with elementary equivalence, definability, and core model-theoretic perspectives.

nodes.title: Proof theory and normalization perspectives
outcomes: Compare proof systems and explain why normalization/cut-elimination style results matter.

nodes.title: Computability, undecidability, and reductions
outcomes: Use reductions conceptually and distinguish undecidability from practical difficulty.

nodes.title: Philosophy of logic: consequence, constants, pluralism, and normativity
outcomes: Compare views about what makes a logic correct or appropriate.

nodes.title: Epistemic disagreement, peer disagreement, polarization, and trust
outcomes: Evaluate rational responses to disagreement and socially mediated evidence.

nodes.title: Bayesian confirmation and alternatives
outcomes: Use Bayesian confirmation concepts while identifying philosophical assumptions and alternatives.

nodes.title: Essence, grounding, fundamentality, and metaphysical explanation
outcomes: Compare contemporary accounts of essence, grounding, and fundamentality.

nodes.title: Metaontology and ontological commitment
outcomes: Analyze disputes over what exists and how ontological commitment is incurred.

nodes.title: Moral realism, anti-realism, constructivism, and expressivism
outcomes: Compare major metaethical positions on truth, objectivity, and moral language.

nodes.title: Decision theory, rational choice, and preference
outcomes: Analyze choice under uncertainty and the normative assumptions of decision models.

nodes.title: Consciousness, representation, and the explanatory gap
outcomes: Compare advanced theories of consciousness and representation.

nodes.title: Semantics-pragmatics boundaries and context sensitivity
outcomes: Analyze how context, semantics, and pragmatic inference interact.

nodes.title: Models, measurement, idealization, and evidence in science
outcomes: Evaluate the epistemic roles of models, measurement, idealization, and data.

nodes.title: Philosophy of technology and artificial intelligence
outcomes: Frame philosophical questions about agency, explanation, automation, and technological mediation.

nodes.title: Philosophy and cognitive science: levels, mechanisms, and explanation
outcomes: Integrate philosophical and cognitive-scientific explanations without collapsing their levels.

nodes.title: Comparative philosophy without false equivalence
outcomes: Compare traditions responsibly while preserving historical and conceptual differences.

nodes.title: Historical interpretation, context, and the principle of charity
outcomes: Balance charitable reconstruction with historical context and textual evidence.

nodes.title: Power, ideology, recognition, race, gender, and social identity
outcomes: Analyze social and political concepts without reducing normative, empirical, and metaphysical questions to one another.

nodes.title: Formal methods as philosophical research tools
outcomes: Use formal systems as tools for precise philosophical modeling and argument.

nodes.title: Argument mapping and computational support for reasoning
outcomes: Build explicit argument graphs and evaluate what computational tools preserve or distort.

nodes.title: Corpus, text, and digital methods for philosophy
outcomes: Use text/corpus methods cautiously for historical or conceptual questions.

nodes.title: Experimental philosophy: design, inference, and limits
outcomes: Evaluate experimental-philosophy studies and separate empirical findings from normative conclusions.

nodes.title: Machine minds, agency, and artificial consciousness
outcomes: Assess arguments about machine mentality, agency, and consciousness.

nodes.title: AI ethics, responsibility, fairness, and sociotechnical power
outcomes: Analyze AI ethics at individual, institutional, and sociotechnical levels.

nodes.title: Philosophy of information and computation
outcomes: Frame information and computation as philosophical concepts rather than mere engineering terms.

nodes.title: Advanced philosophy of mathematics and logic
outcomes: Connect foundational mathematics with advanced philosophy of logic and proof.

nodes.title: Philosophy of physics: space, time, quantum theory, and explanation
outcomes: Analyze philosophical issues arising from physical theory without replacing physics with armchair speculation.

nodes.title: Philosophy of biology: function, species, evolution, and explanation
outcomes: Evaluate concepts of function, species, fitness, and biological explanation.

nodes.title: Social ontology, institutions, law, and collective agency
outcomes: Analyze groups, institutions, norms, and collective agency as ontological and normative problems.

nodes.title: Specialization capstone: one problem across methods and traditions
outcomes: Integrate formal, historical, analytic, and comparative methods on one philosophical problem.

nodes.title: Research literature search, encyclopedias, bibliographies, and citation chains
outcomes: Build a defensible research corpus from reference works, primary texts, papers, and citation chains.

nodes.title: Close reading of primary philosophical texts
outcomes: Produce a textually grounded reconstruction that separates quotation, paraphrase, and interpretation.

nodes.title: Reconstructing an argument at publication-level charity
outcomes: Reconstruct a difficult argument strongly enough that criticism targets its best defensible form.

nodes.title: From puzzle to research question and prospectus
outcomes: Narrow a philosophical puzzle into a researchable question with stakes, literature, and method.

nodes.title: Formal proof, model, or countermodel as philosophical evidence
outcomes: Use a proof, formal model, or countermodel while explaining its philosophical significance and assumptions.

nodes.title: Comparative and cross-tradition research without conceptual flattening
outcomes: Design comparative work that respects linguistic, historical, and conceptual asymmetries.

nodes.title: Peer criticism, objections, revisions, and referee-style response
outcomes: Write and respond to serious objections in a revision-oriented scholarly workflow.

nodes.title: Citation ethics, transparency, reproducibility, and responsible use of sources
outcomes: Maintain transparent provenance and distinguish textual evidence, formal result, empirical evidence, and interpretation.

nodes.title: Build a dated philosophy-and-logic research-frontier map
outcomes: Map active debates and formal frontiers with dated primary and high-quality secondary sources rather than presenting a timeless list.

nodes.title: Formulate an original frontier-level philosophical or logical question
outcomes: Formulate a novel, scoped question with explicit contribution type, literature gap, and evaluation criteria.

nodes.title: Execute an original philosophical paper, formal project, or mixed-method study
outcomes: Carry out an original project with defensible argumentation, evidence, formal work, or empirical method as appropriate.

nodes.title: Produce a contribution-grade portfolio and refresh the frontier
outcomes: Produce a submission-grade artifact, document limitations, and refresh the dated frontier map for future learners.
